articles.title: China watchdog warns Trump faces ‘2-on-1’ showdown with Xi, Putin as Taiwan risks mount
articles.summary: President Donald Trump faces a "two versus one" dynamic with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, who arrive as a team eyeing Taiwan and Ukraine gains.
articles.body: President Donald Trump faces a potentially dangerous "two versus one" negotiating scenario when he meets with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, two senior members of a congressional China watchdog warned Wednesday, raising concerns that Beijing could seek concessions on Taiwan while Moscow pushes for greater U.S. pressure on Ukraine. "I think it is two versus one. We have China and China's junior partner, Russia," Randall Schriver, chairman of the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, told Fox News Digital in a Zoom interview. "Largely they come to the table as a team versus President Trump and the United States," he said, citing China's support for Russia's war in Ukraine. TRUMP ARRIVES IN PHILIPPINES AHEAD OF XI JINPING SUMMIT IN CHINA AFTER GOP MIDTERM LOSSES The warning comes ahead of Thursday's planned trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. The high-stakes talks are expected to address issues such as the wars in Ukraine and Iran, trade and nuclear weapons. Mike Kuiken, the commission's vice chairman, echoed Schriver's assessment, arguing that Moscow's growing dependence on Beijing puts Trump at a disadvantage. "Putin is a client state of Xi Jinping, and that essentially means that President Trump is in the room with a two against one scenario, and the stakes are significant," Kuiken told Fox News Digital. "China is fueling Russia's war machine in Ukraine, and they are basically the lifeblood of the Russian economy at this point," he added. TRUMP TO CONFRONT XI AT HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT OVER CHINA BACKING FOR IRAN, RUSSIA The commissioners spoke as the bipartisan body released its 2026 annual report to Congress, detailing Beijing's expanding military, technological and economic capabilities and the growing challenges they pose to American national security. Asked what would constitute success or failure at the summit, Kuiken suggested Beijing would not have agreed to the meeting without assurances that its interests would be protected. "My assessment is that the Chinese would never have agreed to this meeting if they had not had significant assurances that essentially nothing would happen," Kuiken said. Schriver warned that both Xi and Putin would seek opportunities to advance their strategic objectives. He suggested Beijing would pursue gains related to Taiwan, while Moscow would hope Trump emerged from the meeting prepared to increase pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. CHINA'S XI SURPRISES TRUMP AT TARMAC, RECIPROCATING GESTURE SHOWN MONTHS AGO "If Putin had his way, Trump would emerge from the meeting and put more pressure on Zelenskyy," Schriver said. He also questioned whether sufficient diplomatic groundwork had been laid for meaningful nuclear arms control discussions, one of the issues Trump has indicated he wants to address. "President Trump would like to talk about nuclear disarmament, probably an agenda that makes sense. I'm just not sure we've done the front-end work when it comes to interagency work, bilateral or trilateral work, at a lower level to have a productive discussion there," Schriver said. Nevertheless, Schriver suggested that avoiding concessions could itself represent a successful outcome for Washington. "I think holding ground and just a restatement of U.S. interests is probably a victory of sorts for us," he said. Responding to the commissioners' warnings, a spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington defended the trilateral meeting as an opportunity for cooperation among the three powers. "The three presidents will have an in-depth exchange of views on safeguarding world peace and enabling strategic stability in major-country relations. The summit is of groundbreaking significance," the spokesperson told Fox News Digital. The spokesperson emphasized the three nations' shared responsibilities as permanent members of the U.N. Security Council, arguing that closer communication would serve global stability. "It is in the interest of the three countries to strengthen communication, manage differences and maintain stable relations. This is also the expectation of the international community and is conducive to global stability and dialogue and cooperation," the spokesperson said. CHINA’S IRAN TIES COMPLICATE TRUMP-XI SUMMIT AS TENSIONS TEST US LEVERAGE TAIWAN: 'WE'RE NOT DOING ENOUGH' Beyond the summit, the commissioners warned that the United States faces mounting challenges as China approaches 2027, the benchmark year associated with Xi's directive for the People's Liberation Army to develop the capability to conduct a Taiwan military operation. Asked whether Washington was doing enough to deter Chinese military action against the self-governing island, Schriver gave a blunt assessment. "I think the short answer is no, we're not doing enough," he said. Schriver pointed to a pause in congressional notifications for U.S. arms sales to Taiwan, saying the commission wants those notifications to proceed and supports stronger security assistance for the island. He also warned that Beijing's increasingly sophisticated coercion tactics extend beyond conventional military operations to include actions involving its coast guard. "We do talk about counter coercion capabilities and blending not only military capabilities but law enforcement that the Chinese are doing, this sort of blended lawfare with their coast guard east of Taiwan," Schriver said. "It's a tough challenge as we're entering the benchmark year that Xi Jinping said of 2027. There should be more attention to this and there should be greater efforts to this." Kuiken emphasized Taiwan's importance to the global technology supply chain, particularly its role in manufacturing advanced semiconductors used in artificial intelligence. "Taiwan is the island at the center of the world. Xi Jinping is obsessed with it," he said. Pointing to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, or TSMC, Kuiken warned of the broader implications for American technological leadership if Beijing were to take military action against the island. He urged Washington and its partners to develop a coordinated strategy to make an invasion or other Chinese coercive measures against Taiwan unattractive to Beijing. Responding to concerns about Taiwan, a U.S. official told Fox News Digital, "There is no change to our policy with respect to Taiwan." Asked about the commissioners’ warnings, a White House official emphasized President Trump’s diplomatic approach to China and his plans to discuss nuclear arms reduction during the trilateral summit. "Under President Trump’s leadership, U.S.-China relations have been refocused on what matters most – rebuilding the safety, security and prosperity of Americans. And as President Trump has said: much has been, and will be, accomplished, between the two leaders," the official said. "President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the President of the United States, the President of the People’s Republic of China, and the President of the Russian Federation." "The President has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," the official added. The Chinese Embassy rejected outside involvement in Taiwan's future, reiterating Beijing's claim of sovereignty over the self-governing island. "There is only one China in the world. Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory," the spokesperson said. "The Taiwan question is China's internal affair; how it is resolved is entirely a matter for the Chinese people themselves and brooks no interference from any external forces." The spokesperson added that the U.S. should "exercise extra caution in handling the Taiwan question". TRUMP’S TAIWAN ‘NEGOTIATING CHIP’ REMARK SPARKS ALARM OVER HOW FAR HE'D SHIFT US-CHINA POLICY CHINA'S UNDERSEA THREAT The commissioners also raised alarm about China's rapidly expanding capabilities beneath the ocean, warning that Beijing could threaten the communications infrastructure on which the United States and its allies depend. Asked whether China could disrupt critical American communications during a conflict, Kuiken was unequivocal. "Simple answer is absolutely yes," he said. "The Chinese have spent a long time studying the global communications network and they have absolutely developed the capabilities to sever undersea cables around the globe." Kuiken said he was confident China had probably conducted exercises involving such operations, although he did not identify specific exercises during the interview. Schriver pointed to China's advances in undersea warfare and ocean mapping as among the most concerning developments identified in the commission's research. He said the commission is urging Congress to strengthen protection of undersea communications cables through improved real-time threat detection, rapid repair capabilities and greater coordination with U.S. allies. "So you need to be able to understand in real time when there's a threat to those communication cables," Schriver said. The commission has separately warned that cables linking the United States with Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines are vulnerable to disruption, with damage potentially forcing communications onto slower and less direct routes. The broader concern, Kuiken suggested, is the cumulative effect of China's sustained investment in science and technology at a time when American innovation faces growing competitive pressure. "I think what we are seeing is that the Chinese are starting to turn science, engineering and artificial intelligence into economic strength, national security and global influence," he said. The Chinese Embassy pushed back against framing undersea cable infrastructure as a security threat, arguing that doing so could undermine international connectivity. "Politicizing this issue and turning it into a security one will only disrupt normal international market rules, threaten global digital connectivity and cybersecurity, and serve no one’s interest," the spokesperson said. "China always supports international cooperation on submarine cables under the principles of fairness, justice, equality and inclusiveness, and stands ready to work actively with the rest of the world to promote the building and protection of submarine cables and other global information infrastructure." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP For the two commissioners, those developments underscore the stakes of Trump's meeting with Xi and Putin: Washington faces not only an immediate diplomatic challenge but a longer-term competition with a Chinese leadership that is steadily building the capabilities to challenge American power.

articles.title: Pew Research: Islam on track to become world’s largest religion by 2035
articles.summary: The report projects steady increases for both Christianity and Islam from 2020 to 2070.
articles.body:
Islam will soon be the world’s largest religion, taking Christianity’s place by 2035, according to the Pew Research Center.

The research organisation assessed the Muslim population’s expected growth in a report released on Tuesday, which projected that both groups will see their numbers increase over the next few decades.

However, the Muslim population will “simply [grow] at a faster pace,” the report said.

The projection analysed 201 countries and territories, accounting for 99.98 percent of the population, and spanned the geographic distribution and future changes of seven religious groups and affiliations – Muslims, Christians, Jews, Hindus, Buddhists, and others – from the years 2020 to 2070.

The results are part of the Pew-Templeton Global Religious Futures Project, which seeks to analyse religious change and its impact on the world.

The organisation stressed that the findings are “not intended to predict all the ways the world could change” as several other events might occur that could impact a group’s religious affiliation, such as socioeconomic circumstances, natural disasters, and wars.

According to the report, Muslims give birth to the highest number of children, one of the factors that Pew says make them the world’s fastest-growing religious group.

Fertility rates were found to be 3.1 children per Muslim woman, while Christians, with the second-highest fertility rate, had 2.5 children per Christian woman.

A generation can typically replace itself with a fertility rate of around 2.1 children per woman.

Both groups are expected to “keep pace with the world’s overall population growth”, according to Pew.

Muslims could gain up to 1.6 billion people through natural population change, compared to 792 million people for Christians.

Muslims are expected to have much smaller losses in their community than Christians leaving or converting religions.

“The difference between the number of people who join and leave Islam is expected to result in a loss of 8 million people during the projection period, [whereas] for Christians, the net difference is a projected loss of 105 million people,” the report said.

Those who choose to depart from Christianity may not identify with a religion afterwards, including atheists and agnostics.

However, the research finds that Islam’s projected growth is not the result of people converting from Christianity: the number of Muslims projected to convert to Christianity is only “slightly greater” than the number of Christians expected to become Muslims.

Between 2020 and 2070, “most of the growth in the world’s Muslim population is projected to occur in places where Muslims already make up a majority of the population”, said Pew.

By 2070, Muslims will make up 95 percent of the population in the Middle East-North Africa region. Meanwhile, in the Asia-Pacific region, Muslims are expected to surpass the religiously unaffiliated.

Muslims were the majority religious group in 53 countries in 2020. An additional 1.2 billion Muslims are expected to live in these countries by 2070, representing 74 percent of the projected growth of the global Muslim population.

For instance, Pakistan’s Muslim population is expected to double from 227 million in 2020 to 461 million in 2070. The country will become the world’s largest Muslim population, overtaking Indonesia, Pew said.

Christian growth will also be concentrated across 120 countries where Christians were already the majority of the population.

Overall, the population of Christians in these countries is forecast to rise by 630 million, representing 92 percent of global Christian growth.

articles.title: What does Israel’s new ground offensive mean for Palestinians in Gaza?
articles.summary: Israeli tanks advance beyond the ‘Yellow Line’, forcing Palestinians to flee again in Gaza.
articles.body:
Israeli forces have launched a ground operation in central Gaza, advancing west of the line they withdrew to under last year’s ceasefire and forcing Palestinian families, many of whom had already been displaced, to flee their homes once again.

The operation, the first major ground offensive publicly announced by the Israeli military since the ceasefire took effect on October 10, 2025, follows a warning by the United States-backed Board of Peace that the 13-month-old agreement risks collapse. In a report to the United Nations Security Council, the board accused Israel of restricting aid and delaying the deployment of Palestinian police, and Hamas of continuing armed activity and taxing goods entering Gaza. Senior Hamas official Basem Naim dismissed the report as “pure disinformation”.

What happened in central Gaza on Wednesday?

Israeli tanks and bulldozers advanced towards Salah al-Din Street, Gaza’s main north-south route, east of the Nuseirat refugee camp and north of the Bureij refugee camp, Al Jazeera correspondents reported. Palestinians fled those areas, amid heavy gunfire and artillery shelling.

The Israeli military body overseeing civilian affairs in the occupied Palestinian territory, known as COGAT, said the army had closed that stretch of Salah al-Din Street and told residents to stay away until further notice. The army hasn’t said how long the operation will last.

An Israeli attack on al-Mughraqa killed one person and wounded several others, an official at al-Awda Hospital told Al Jazeera. Separate attacks in Deir el-Balah, Nuseirat and Gaza City killed three more people.

“We fear this may be the start of a broader operation and that displacement will begin anew, as we have not yet recovered from the effects of the previous war and displacement,” Mahmoud al-Saafin, a 27-year-old resident of Bureij, told the AFP news agency.

The areas targeted in the operation lie west of the “Yellow Line”, where Israeli troops pulled back to under the first phase of President Donald Trump’s plan, leaving them in about 53 percent of Gaza. Israel has, however, continued to move that line gradually, and it now encompasses around two-thirds of the enclave. More than two million Palestinians live in the rest, mostly in tents.

Why does Israel say it launched the operation?

The military told AFP it had launched “a precise operation” west of the line “to remove a threat” posed to the Israeli army, adding that “there is Hamas infrastructure in the area, adding it was responding to Hamas ceasefire violations.

“We reserve the freedom to act and manoeuvre whenever necessary to eliminate any immediate threat in the Gaza Strip,” the army said.

Israel says Hamas has been regrouping and rearming, and it has stepped up attacks. On Saturday, an Israeli attack killed Samir Abu Younis, the Qassam Brigades’ Rafah commander.

Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said Israel won’t withdraw until Hamas is dismantled. “If tensions escalate on the various fronts, we are fully prepared to seize additional territory, evacuate local residents and incorporate it into Israel’s permanent security perimeter,” he said.

How have Palestinian groups, including Hamas, responded?

Hamas called the operation and the forced evacuations northeast of Nuseirat “a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement”, and urged mediators to “intervene immediately”.

It accused Israel of “systematically” squeezing Palestinians into a narrow area of Gaza, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s caretaker government of escalating to escape its domestic crises.

Hamas also condemned the Board of Peace for having “unacceptably equated the occupation’s ongoing aggression with the suffering of the Palestinian victim”.

The Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine called the operation a “prelude” to a wider escalation aimed at forcibly displacing Palestinians.

Has Israel violated the Gaza ceasefire before?

Israeli forces have kept up near-daily attacks, shelling and home demolitions. Gaza’s Ministry of Health says they have killed 1,658 Palestinians and wounded 6,000 since the ceasefire began. The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed in the same period, the Reuters news agency reports.

On Tuesday alone, Israeli fire killed six Palestinians, including a six-year-old boy, Gaza’s civil defence agency and hospitals told AFP.

Aid remains restricted. About 100,000 tents are waiting to enter Gaza, held up by crossing closures and lengthy Israeli security checks, the International Organization for Migration says.

The ceasefire halted major fighting, but the rest of the plan, covering Israel’s withdrawal, reconstruction and Hamas’s disarmament, has stalled. Hamas agreed in July to a roadmap to give up its weapons and hand over governance. Israel rejected it.

Israel also hasn’t let the board’s technocratic administration start work in Gaza. That has held up an international stabilisation force, The Associated Press news agency reported.

The board spelled out what failure would mean. “Should it collapse, there would be no road map to return to, no administration to deploy and no enabling environment to rebuild.”

articles.title: Prince Harry, after Ukraine trip, warns on threat from Russia
articles.summary: The Duke of Sussex thought people should be ready to serve again for their country if needed.
articles.body:
The Duke of Sussex, who carried out a surprise visit to Ukraine at the weekend , has said he would rejoin the military if asked, as he warned of the threat from Russia.

He told the Telegraph he thought people were right to be nervous in the current international political climate and said it was time to "double our support" for Ukraine.

There appeared to be warnings about President Trump - with Prince Harry saying there was a big separation between what the American public thinks about Ukraine and the administration's attitude.

Prince Harry, able to speak more freely than working royals, said he hoped after the US mid-term elections it would be "fantastic to have more American support" for Ukraine.

Speaking to the Telegraph's Dominic Nicholls, Prince Harry said he thought the threat to Europe had been there for the past 15 years - and he felt like it had been at war for the past decade.

"Just because there's not drones, bullets, and rockets flying at us, it doesn't mean that we're not at war," said Prince Harry.

Prince Harry had been in Lviv in Ukraine on Saturday and Sunday - and had told the BBC and journalists at events that he thought the "rest of the world will continue to support" Ukraine.

He had told his Ukrainian hosts, about a conflict with Russia that has already lasted more than four years: "You're going to win the war."

In his Telegraph podcast, he called for a similar unity that was being shown by Ukraine, and feared that Europe could be divided and could "turn on itself".

He addressed the shifting position of US President Trump in a way that is unusual for a royal.

"I think there's been a big separation between what American society feels regarding support for Ukraine, which I think is incredibly high and always has been, compared to a certain group, or in, in this case, an administration that was perhaps thinking about it differently," said Prince Harry.

"As of January, things are going to change, so I think we should all be looking forward to that," he said, referring to the US mid-term elections, which saw significant setbacks for President Trump.

The BBC has approached the White House for comment.

Having served in the military in Afghanistan, Harry said he would return if needed for a future conflict: "If asked to sign up again, if the need is there, then I will 100% be there to serve my country alongside my fellow veterans and service personnel."

Prince Harry had received an enthusiastic welcome when he visited Lviv in Ukraine at the weekend, meeting Ukrainian competitors taking part in his Invictus Games.

There were emotional scenes as he was applauded by injured service men and women, some of the 150,000 seriously wounded war veterans in the country.

His visit had been carried out with a press blackout for security reasons - and the night before journalists arrived in the city to cover the visit, there had been air raid warnings that had forced Prince Harry's planning team to head for the shelters.

"Ukraine now is experiencing elements of war that no other country has experienced before," Prince Harry had said, including inventing new ways of treating the growing number of injured casualties.

"War is a terrible thing," he said in Lviv, but hailed the resilience of the Ukrainians who had been badly wounded in their defence against Russia's invasion.

articles.title: Man accused of attacking Northwestern student followed others from train to dorms
articles.summary: A man who is accused of attempting to strangle a Northwestern University student in her dorm room got into the building after following two other students to the campus from the train, prosecutors said.
articles.body: A man who is accused of attempting to strangle a Northwestern University student in her dorm room got into the building after following two other students to the campus from the train, prosecutors said. Prosecutors said two Northwestern students were on the Red Line heading home from the city around 4:30 p.m. on Sunday when they saw a man in the same train car, later identified as 23-year-old Diaunte Adams, watching them. As the two students switched from the Red Line to the Purple Line, Adams allegedly followed them. Then, when they got off at the Noyes train stop, Adams allegedly followed them off the train and all the way to campus, prosecutors said. The two students reached out to a friend who lives in a nearby dorm, Elder Hall, and asked if they could be let in. The friend let the two students into the building, prosecutors said, but the door closed slowly enough for Adams to enter the building behind them. The three students then ran into a dorm room and called the police, prosecutors said. Security footage showed Adams entering an elevator in the dorm building that he used to travel to the fourth floor, prosecutors said. When he exited the building, a student was in the hallway returning to her dorm. Adams allegedly followed her down the hall and into her room before she was able to close the door. The student asked Adams if he was OK, prosecutors said, and he allegedly shook his head no. The “terrified” student then tried to get past Adams to escape the situation and was only able to wedge her foot into the door to keep it partially open before Adams grabbed her and wrapped his arms around her chest and neck, prosecutors alleged. She screamed for help until Adams held her so tightly that she was unable to scream or breathe and began to lose consciousness, prosecutors said. Her screams were heard by other students and several of them came running to her door. “Me and Logan [Rogers] were studying, and Andrew [Kim] was watching a football game, and then all of a sudden we heard frantic screaming,” freshman student Lucas Gonzalez told NBC Chicago. “We went into the room and then the first thing we all see is a girl with her foot sticking out wedging the door so the guy doesn’t lock her in.” Rogers said that when he and the others got there, Adams had his hands around the woman’s neck. “We all pushed collectively and we got in and we saw her getting choked and then we separated them,” Gonzalez said. After getting the woman away from Adams, two of the men shut the door to the room and trapped him inside, prosecutors said. They held the door shut until police arrived and arrested Adams. The three students, now being called heroes by many, said they don’t see themselves as such. “We knew someone was in trouble and I think anyone in our situation would have tried to do the same thing,” Kim said. Cellphone video captured Adams being taken out of the dorm building by authorities. The woman who was attacked was taken to a local hospital, where she was treated for injuries to her neck and leg. Adams now faces charges including criminal trespassing, home invasion and aggravated battery, prosecutors said. After the attack, Northwestern University issued a statement saying they increased security presence on campus. No additional information was immediately available.

articles.summary: The U.S. Army is hiring contractors to build 17 reinforced concrete bunkers in Israel, Saudi Arabia and Lebanon amid Iranian missile and drone attacks.
articles.body: The U.S. Army is racing to hire contractors to build 17 reinforced concrete bunkers in Israel, Saudi Arabia and Lebanon to protect American and coalition troops from deadly missile and drone attacks, according to a government procurement notice posted Friday. The move comes amid escalating violence in the Middle East, where Iranian attacks on U.S. military installations have killed at least 23 American service members since war broke out in late February. On Tuesday, Iran also claimed responsibility for another strike on a U.S. military base in Bahrain, its third attack there in five days. BAHRAIN INTERCEPTS IRANIAN DRONES TARGETING US RADAR AFTER 2-MONTH LULL IN GULF STRIKES Kuwaiti air defenses also intercepted incoming drones as Israeli forces launched new strikes in eastern and southern Lebanon. The Army plans to build 10 bunkers in Israel, five in Saudi Arabia and two in Lebanon, replacing makeshift shelters made from shipping containers. "Due to elevated regional force protection conditions, there is an urgent, high-priority requirement to replace nonstandard personnel protection shelters (e.g., converted shipping containers) and provide standardized, precast, reinforced concrete Indirect Fire bunkers," the Army said in the notice. "The objective is to safeguard U.S. and coalition service members operating in potentially hostile environments across multiple countries in [U.S. Central Command] Area of Responsibility," the notice added. PENTAGON JUMPS FROM $225M TO $55B ON DRONES AS CHEAP ATTACKS OVERWHELM US DEFENSES The effort also follows a series of Iranian missile and drone attacks on U.S. bases across the Persian Gulf. A March drone strike on a U.S. Army command post at Kuwait's Port of Shuaiba killed six American service members, with reports saying the facility lacked adequate protection against aerial attacks. President Donald Trump said Nov. 16 that defensive measures had been effective across the region. "Iran has fired between 8,000-9,000 One-way Attack Drones. Only 2 of them got through, resulting in U.S. fatalities, both on the first day, hitting Kuwait and Saudi Arabia. Likewise, Iran has fired about 2,000 Ballistic Missiles. Only 1 out of the 2,0000 got through, and caused U.S. fatalities (Jordan)," he wrote on Truth Social. [U.S. Central Command] defensive measures have been historically effective. No one in the World has the ability to do so well. All of this being left out of the 60 Minutes ‘report,’" he added. The 17 bunkers will be built at five military installations: one in Israel and two each in Saudi Arabia and Lebanon, the notice said. The Army is withholding the sites' locations for security reasons, saying names and coordinates will be provided only to eligible contractors once the formal solicitation is issued. Each bunker will have three precast, reinforced concrete sections, steel entrance doors shielded by concrete barriers and sandbag-reinforced exterior walls. Each roof will be covered with at least 18 inches of layered sandbags to protect against incoming fire. "Due to extreme operational urgency (soldiers currently at risk using non-standard containerized shelters), the subsequent solicitation is anticipated to have an expedited 3-day quote turnaround window," the Army said. articles.title: 35 yrs on, a landmark moment: Forces kill Kashmir's last active local terrorist
articles.summary: SRINAGAR/NEW DELHI: Security forces killed 22-year-old Lashkar-e-Taiba terrorist Mohammad Lateef Bhat in a shootout outside a mosque in Kulgam district
articles.body: SRINAGAR/NEW DELHI: Security forces killed 22-year-old Lashkar-e-Taiba terrorist Mohammad Lateef Bhat in a shootout outside a mosque in Kulgam district early Wednesday, ending a weeklong hunt and eliminating Kashmir's last known active local terrorist, according to J&K police.The killing marked what police described as a watershed moment in Kashmir's 35-year fight against terrorism, dealing a blow to Pakistan's efforts to project terrorist violence in the Valley as a home-grown movement. It also marked a turning point in Kashmir's counterterror campaign, with police saying local recruitment into terrorist ranks had fallen to almost zero. Home minister Amit Shah hailed the operation as a coordinated success of J&K police, Army, CRPF and intelligence agencies, saying Bhat was Lashkar's last known active local terrorist in the valley.Bhat refused to surrender, was killed trying to escapeLateef Bhat, who carried a Rs 15 lakh bounty, was killed outside a mosque in Zangalpora village after a week-long chase across south Kashmir. His associate, Nisar, a new recruit, was killed near Larnoo bypass on Nov 16.J&K Police DG Nalin Prabhat called it a milestone in the fight against three decades of terrorism, saying local recruitment had fallen to almost zero. Only two Kashmiri youths joined LeT in the past two years, he said, adding that the force was working to dismantle the terrorist ecosystem. “We have been fighting Pakistan-sponsored terrorism for the past 35 years,” Prabhat said.Lieutenant governor Manoj Sinha said only a handful of foreign terrorists remained and J&K would soon be terrorism-free.Home minister Amit Shah posted on X, “Lateef Bhat was neutralised in an operation in Kulgam in the early morning hours. One of his terrorist associates, Umar Nisar, was also neutralised in Kulgam, the day before. The entire operation was marked by a very high level of synergy. The nation salutes the brave Jawans.”Local recruitment has fluctuated sharply over the years. The number fell from 54 in 2010 to 16 in 2013 before climbing to 53 in 2014, 66 in 2015, 88 in 2016 and 126 in 2017, according to security agencies. It peaked at 196 in 2018, declined to 143 in 2019 and rose again to 174 in 2020. Of those recruited in 2020, 76 were killed and 46 arrested. In 2021, 128 local youths joined terrorist groups — 73 were killed and 16 arrested.Bhat’s killing followed a cat-and-mouse chase that began after the Nov 11 attack on a CRPF picket in Kulgam, in which three personnel were wounded. Human intelligence, CCTV footage, cyber surveillance and details from a phone Bhat had dropped while fleeing helped security forces trace him.Bhat, a resident of Khrewan Chader village in Kulgam, had been wanted for the killing of a J&K police head constable in Anantnag and two migrant workers in Kulgam in July. He had escaped a shootout in Shopian in July, when his LeT associate, Zakir Ganie, was killed.Security forces cornered the duo in Kulgam on Nov 16. Nisar was killed near Larnoo bypass, but Bhat escaped, discarding his clothes to evade the cordon. He was traced to Jamia Mosque in Zangalpora Tuesday. Police cordoned off the area around 11pm.Kulgam SSP Anayat Ali Choudhary said security forces made repeated attempts to persuade Bhat to surrender, including a video call. Mosque committee members were also sent inside to convince him to lay down his arms. “We told him that he was still young and should surrender but he refused,” Choudhary said.Bhat opened fire around 3.45am Wednesday. Choudhary said forces exercised maximum restraint because Bhat was inside a mosque in the cordoned-off area. Bhat was killed outside the religious structure while attempting to escape. Unlike earlier operations, there was little local support for him.Bhat left his home in Nov 2025, prompting his family to file a missing-person report. He was recruited into LeT and its proxy, The Resistance Front. He also allegedly operated under Kashmir Revolutionary Army, an outfit used in attempts to sustain local recruitment.CRPF chief GP Singh congratulated personnel, saying: “Some dishes are best served cold, even in cold weather.” J&K Police posted, “You can run but cannot hide.”Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A Canadian couple built a deck at their British Columbia resort cabin without written approval; their resort manager wanted it demolished, but a November 13 appeals ruling let it stay with a $5,000 payment
articles.summary: A Canadian couple who built a wooden deck beside their holiday cabin without obtaining the required written permission have won a legal battle to keep the
articles.body: A Canadian couple who built a wooden deck beside their holiday cabin without obtaining the required written permission have won a legal battle to keep the structure after a British Columbia appeals court upheld a $5,000 damages award instead of ordering its removal. The November 13 decision in Valley’s Edge Park Ltd. v. Holden followed a dispute between the homeowners and the company overseeing their recreational resort. The British Columbia Court of Appeal’s judgment, its official case summary and reporting by Canadian Legal News provide details of the ruling. Moira and Denis Holden owned a property at Valley’s Edge Resort in Edgewater, British Columbia, where residents are required to seek approval before making certain improvements to their lots. The requirement is part of a registered building scheme that gives the resort administrator authority over construction and alterations. The couple had previously obtained permission for improvements to another property they owned at the resort. However, their relationship with the company’s president later deteriorated, and a disagreement over the proposed deck eventually reached the courts.How the dispute beganIn 2022, the Holdens approached the elected president of the strata council with their plans for the deck. They were informed that the council did not have the authority to approve the construction. Although the plans were subsequently forwarded to the company, the couple had already completed the work by then.Valley’s Edge Park Ltd. gave them 30 days to either dismantle the deck or submit a complete application for approval. The couple responded with a hand-drawn diagram, but the company’s president rejected it, describing the submission as incomplete.The matter became contentious when the company sought to have the structure removed. However, the judge who first heard the dispute found that the company’s president had not clearly explained what information was missing from the application or what changes would make it acceptable. The court also considered the appearance and impact of the deck. It found that the structure was consistent with the cabin and the surrounding resort environment. There was also no evidence that it prevented neighbouring property owners from accessing or enjoying their own lots.Why the court allowed the deck to remainThe resort administrator argued that allowing the structure to remain would set an undesirable precedent, potentially encouraging other property owners to construct unauthorised improvements before seeking permission.The court acknowledged that the Holdens had knowingly proceeded without the necessary approval. However, it also considered whether demolishing the deck was necessary to protect the interests of the wider resort community. An injunction, which is a court order requiring someone to stop or take a particular action, is generally the preferred remedy for breaches of registered building schemes. However, the court can consider the circumstances of an individual case before deciding whether removal is appropriate.The judge concluded that financial compensation would be sufficient in this instance. Valley’s Edge had sought $20,000 in damages, while the couple maintained that they had spent approximately $1,800 building the deck themselves and argued that only nominal compensation should be awarded. The court ultimately ordered the Holdens to pay $5,000. Neither side challenged the amount in the subsequent appeal.Both sides lose their appealsValley’s Edge Park Ltd. challenged the decision, arguing that the judge should have ordered the deck’s removal and that the company was entitled to recover its entire legal bill from the homeowners. The Holdens also challenged the original costs order, arguing that they should not have been required to pay the resort administrator’s legal expenses.However, the British Columbia Court of Appeal dismissed both appeals in its November 13 ruling. Justice DeWitt-Van Oosten, writing for a unanimous panel, found no reason to overturn the lower court’s decision to award damages instead of ordering an injunction. The judges also rejected the company’s argument that the building scheme automatically entitled it to recover all its legal fees. Although the agreement allowed the administrator to recover expenses associated with work undertaken to correct a breach, its wording was not sufficiently clear to make homeowners responsible for every legal expense incurred while pursuing an injunction.The original costs award in favour of Valley’s Edge was therefore upheld, as the company had successfully established that the couple breached the building scheme and obtained damages. For the appeal proceedings, the court ordered each side to pay the other’s costs for defending the respective appeal. Both amounts will be assessed at Scale A, reflecting the court’s view that the parties had made the proceedings more complicated than necessary.The ruling leaves the deck standing, but it also reinforces that property owners cannot simply disregard construction approval requirements. Even when demolition is considered unnecessary, building without permission can still carry financial consequences.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: GTA 6 release: Nearly 1 in 5 US workers plan to take time off to play
articles.summary: Nearly one in five salaried workers in the United States plans to take time off for the release of Grand Theft Auto 6 on Thursday, November 19.
articles.body: Nearly one in five salaried workers in the United States plans to take time off for the release of Grand Theft Auto 6 on Thursday, November 19. Some have already booked their paid leave, while others are considering calling in sick to spend the day playing the long-awaited game. A GameSquare survey also found that 36% of workers considering time off would rather call in sick than request leave. The trend, being called the ‘GTA flu’ online, comes after players waited 13 years for a new game in the popular franchise.Lander Allgood and Connor Folkers plan extended breaks for GTA 6 releaseFor some players, the GTA 6 launch is worth planning their entire week around. Lander Allgood, a 26-year-old environmental specialist from the Dallas-Fort Worth area, requested two weeks of paid time off in July so he could enjoy the release.Allgood, who has played GTA 5 since he was around 13, compared the new game’s arrival to a major scientific achievement.“We’re basically witnessing, I mean, the Apollo space program of video games,” Allgood told USA TODAY.However, gaming is not his only responsibility. He plans to spend time with his two-year-old son and has arranged for his parents to look after the child from Thursday through Sunday. Once his son goes to bed, Allgood expects to spend hours playing. He is hoping to put in at least 20 hours over the weekend.Connor Folkers, a 22-year-old IT administrator from Iowa, has also arranged his schedule around the launch. He requested leave from November 19 through Thanksgiving and expects to spend more than 24 hours playing.For Folkers, getting enough time with the game before seeing other people’s reactions is important. He wants to experience the story and gameplay without online discussions shaping his opinion.“Really how I treat this game is sort of like a cultural event. You’re going to see this, I presume, everywhere online, whether it be story components or gameplay components, so I want to make sure I have enough time to really experience it for myself without the outside influencing my opinions on it,” Folkers told USA TODAY.He also compared the release to the Super Bowl, explaining how important the event has become for gaming enthusiasts.GTA flu: Why some gamers are planning to call in sickNot everyone is being upfront about taking a day off. Some players are planning to report sick on November 19 instead of requesting paid leave in advance.GameSquare surveyed 1,000 full-time US employees who identified as gamers. Its findings showed that 10% planned to skip work on launch day, while another 30% were considering taking time off. Among those considering leave, 36% said they would call in sick.BambooHR also found that nearly one in five salaried US workers planned to take time off for the release. Its figures showed that 32% of Gen Z employees and 27% of millennials intended to use paid leave to play.Nicole Csiszar, BambooHR’s director of HR, told USA TODAY that taking planned leave is a normal way for employees to enjoy their time away from work.“That’s a healthy sign,” Csiszar told USA TODAY. “It means people are using PTO the way it’s meant to be used, to step away and do something they enjoy.”She also pointed out why some might choose to call in sick instead.“Requesting PTO in advance means submitting it, waiting on approval and sometimes explaining why you want the day,” Csiszar told USA TODAY. “Calling in sick is one message that morning.”However, not every gamer is willing to put work aside. Ryan Van Dusen, a 42-year-old fifth-grade teacher from Michigan, has no plans to miss classes for the game. He is instead looking forward to playing during the Thanksgiving holiday.“My kids are expected to be in the classroom. I can’t take a day off from my students for this. This is preposterous,” Van Dusen told USA TODAY with a laugh. “In theory, Grand Theft Auto should be a small thing compared to work, family, things that are bigger. I think it’s healthy and good for us to have these small things that we can be excited for too and just to look forward to.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Iraq sentences six French nationals to life in prison for joining ISIL
articles.summary: Trials began in September for 47 French citizens who were transferred from Syria last year.
articles.body:
An Iraqi criminal court has sentenced six French nationals to life in prison for joining the ISIL (ISIS) group, state media reported.

The Karkh Criminal Court delivered the sentencing on Wednesday with representatives from the French embassy in attendance, the Iraqi News Agency (INA) reported, citing Iraq’s judiciary.

“With these six sentences, the total number of those convicted in this case has reached 16, all of whom are French nationals,” the judiciary said in a statement cited by INA.

All but one of the 16 convicted were sentenced to life. The court sentenced one defendant to 15 years in prison last month.

Trials began in September for 47 French citizens who were transferred from Syria last year and charged with belonging to the armed group, which controlled large parts of both countries between 2014 and 2017.

In February, Iraq received more than 5,700 ISIL detainees from over 60 countries after the United States transferred them from Syria, following years of detention in prisons run by Kurdish-led forces.

For years, Iraqi courts handed down hundreds of execution orders and life sentences to people convicted of “terrorism” offences, including foreign fighters. However, some rights groups denounced the trials as rushed and lacking due process.

Among the foreign fighters sentenced on Wednesday was Thomas Barnouin, a 45-year-old Frenchman, who said during his trial that he travelled to Syria convinced he had a religious duty and did not know ISIL would carry out attacks in France, according to AFP.

The ISIL group swept across Syria and Iraq in 2014, committing massacres and forcing women and girls into sexual slavery.

Iraq, backed by US-led forces, proclaimed victory over the group in 2017, and Kurdish-led forces supported by Washington defeated ISIL in neighbouring Syria two years later.

Iraq is nonetheless still reckoning with the group’s legacy, with mass graves being uncovered and testimonies of its brutality still to be investigated.

articles.title: American couple started Yellow Leaf Hammocks as a side hustle from their Volkswagen after discovering handwoven hammocks in Thailand; the business later reached $1 million in monthly revenue and $30 million in lifetime sales
articles.summary: Yellow Leaf Hammocks, the handmade hammock company founded by the Los Angeles couple Joe Demin and Rachel Connors, began as a side hustle run from the
articles.body: Yellow Leaf Hammocks, the handmade hammock company founded by the Los Angeles couple Joe Demin and Rachel Connors, began as a side hustle run from the back of their Volkswagen. Started in 2011 and funded from its own sales, the business reached $1 million in monthly revenue in 2023 and passed $30 million in lifetime sales by 2024. The American husband and wife built the brand on hammocks handwoven by women in Thailand and, by 2024, had sold to more than 100,000 customers. Demin worked in real estate finance and Connors in nonprofit fundraising while they built the company together.How a holiday in Thailand and a hammock outside a hut inspired Joe Demin to start Yellow LeafAccording to Entrepreneur, the idea took shape in 2011, when Demin went on holiday to Thailand and found a hammock he considered the world’s comfiest outside a tiny hut on an island in the Andaman Sea. The company’s own website says the discovery came during an impromptu motorcycle adventure, and that the hammocks were unlike anything he had seen or felt before.He bought as many as he could fit in his backpack and headed home with a business plan written on an airsickness bag. There he teamed up with Connors, now his wife, to establish the business. Demin wanted to back the weavers’ vision and build a brand that captured the relaxed feeling of that first hammock.Meet the Mlabri craftswomen of Northern Thailand who handweave every Yellow Leaf hammockYellow Leaf Hammocks’ website says each hammock is handwoven by expert craftswomen of the Mlabri Tribe, a name that translates to “the people of the yellow leaves”, in the hills of Northern Thailand. Across three weaving communities, the company says it creates jobs for mothers and cuts out the middleman so that money goes directly to its weavers.It argues that jobs for women matter especially, citing research that women spend up to 90 per cent of their income on their families’ health, nutrition and education. It adds that becoming breadwinners builds self-esteem, improves women’s standing in their communities, and lets them pool resources to improve local infrastructure. The weavers it profiles include Song, a dedicated mother who prioritises her children’s schooling, and Daeng, one of the few Mlabri men to weave hammocks.How a tent at a weekly arts market and reinvested profits delivered the first 1,000 hammock salesThe couple took those first hammocks to a weekly arts market near their home, put up a tent and met their first customers face to face. Each week they reinvested their profits in inventory for the next fair. They sold their first 1,000 hammocks that way, asking buyers what they wanted and which parts of the brand story resonated.Money was tight. Demin and Connors chose to build the brand through revenue rather than chase investment, wanting to reach a certain level of success before approaching investors so they could protect their mission. The business was cash-flow positive from the start, though growth was slow, and it generated about $100,000 in its first year. Along the way, they taught themselves everything from textile engineering and wholesale pricing to coding a website.How the pandemic hit the wholesale business and a Shark Tank appearance sparked a switch onlineAfter going through a business incubator, the couple focused on getting picked up by retailers. They collaborated with names including CB2, Anthropologie and Tommy Bahama and built what Connors considered a strong wholesale operation. The pandemic then devastated their business with brick-and-mortar retailers.When the chance came to appear on Shark Tank in 2020, they moved quickly to become an online business. Within months, they had changed from a wholesale company into a direct-to-consumer brand, which let them communicate more directly with customers and build deeper relationships with their fans.How the company’s mission grew from helping a couple of dozen weavers to training hundredsThe mission began small, with Demin and Connors hoping to help a couple of dozen women. By 2024, they had trained hundreds of weavers and employed hundreds of full-time artisans in rural Thailand. Some weavers’ children had gone on to college on the strength of hammock income.Demin and Connors told Entrepreneur that building a social enterprise that changes weavers’ lives is the most fulfilling part of the work, while Connors enjoys the creativity and daily hustle of entrepreneurship. Their advice for aspiring founders starts with a simple rule: “know your numbers”. Demin calls them the lifeblood of a company, since a great product or meaningful mission counts for little without profitability. Connors urges founders to stay close to customer service and to ask customers for their opinions and ideas, because that is where direct insights come from.You use AI every day. articles.title: U.K.’s Prince Harry sees ‘big separation’ between U.S. administration, public on support for Ukraine
articles.summary: LONDON — Britain’s Prince Harry offered a veiled criticism of the U.S. government’s policy toward Ukraine, saying in an interview released late Wednesday that he believes there is a “big separation” between the Trump Administration’s stance and that of the American people.
articles.body: LONDON — Britain’s Prince Harry offered a veiled criticism of the U.S. government’s policy toward Ukraine, saying in an interview released late Wednesday that he believes there is a “big separation” between the Trump Administration’s stance and that of the American people. Harry, a British Army veteran who returned to his home country last summer after six years in California, also said he believes Britain has been in conflict with Russia for the past decade and that he is ready to serve in the military once again if he is called upon to do so. The comments came in an interview with The Daily Telegraph that took place last weekend during Harry’s fourth visit to Ukraine since the full-scale Russian invasion. The newspaper published a story about the interview on Wednesday and is scheduled to release the full interview in a podcast that will be posted at midnight London time (0000 GMT). “I think there’s been a big separation between what American society feel regarding support for Ukraine, which I think is incredibly high and always has been, compared to a certain group, or in this case an administration, that was perhaps thinking about it differently,” Harry said. Harry traveled to Ukraine last weekend to meet with athletes who are preparing to take part in the 2027 Invictus Games, the Paralympic-style competition he founded to inspire wounded veterans. Next year’s games will take place in Birmingham, England. The prince is not a working member of the royal family and traveled to Ukraine as a private citizen. Harry said now is the time for Britain and its allies to double their support for Ukraine to ensure that it defeats Russia at a time when Moscow is trying to stir up divisions within European society. British intelligence and military officials are increasingly warning about sabotage, disinformation campaigns and other so-called hybrid attacks carried out by Russian operatives to destabilize western societies. “I think the threat has been there and been consistently there for the last 15 years,” Harry said. “Just because there’s not drones, bullets and rockets flying at us, that doesn’t mean that we’re not at war. I feel like we’ve been at war for the last decade.” Harry, who was deployed to Afghanistan twice during his military career, said veterans should be ready to serve again. “If the need is there, then I will 100% be there to serve my country, alongside my fellow veterans and service personnel,” he said.

articles.title: Man accused of Central Park rapes makes first New York City court appearance
articles.summary: A man arrested in Florida and accused of multiple Central Park rapes made his first New York City court appearance on Wednesday as prosecutors said they have DNA evidence and eyewitness identifications against him.
articles.body: A man arrested in Florida and accused of multiple Central Park rapes made his first New York City court appearance on Wednesday as prosecutors said they have DNA evidence and eyewitness identifications against him. Dereck Rivera-Deleon, 30, who did not enter a plea, was ordered held without bail. Rivera-Deleon, who was arrested this month in Miami, has been charged in sexual assault attacks in Central Park this year and in 2021. Authorities said they are investigating a possible third attack in the park, in 2023, though prosecutors said they have not yet filed charges in that case. Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg said his office would continue to investigate. “Dereck Rivera-Deleon was just arraigned on two horrific allegations of rape and remanded without bail,” he said in a prepared statement. “We are continuing to investigate a third allegation, all committed within a span of half a decade in Central Park. New Yorkers deserve to use our parks safely and without fear.” A court-appointed defense lawyer declined to speak to reporters outside court following Wednesday’s hearing. Rivera-Deleon was ordered to return to court on Nov. 23.

articles.title: US steps up pressure on Iran-backed Hezbollah with new sanctions
articles.summary: The US Treasury has accused Hezbollah of using charitable organisations as ‘fronts’ for fundraising.
articles.body:
The ‌‌United States has announced new sanctions targeting a group that it says serves as a “front organisation” for the Lebanese group Hezbollah, which Washington considers a “terrorist” entity.

On Wednesday, the US Treasury said it had designated the Wa Ta’awanu Association, named for the Arabic words for “and cooperate”, the first two words of a popular Quranic verse.

It described the organisation as a “Hizballah-affiliated charity that provides cover for Hizballah’s activities under the guise of delivering humanitarian services”.

Three people based ⁠⁠in Lebanon were also sanctioned. They include the Wa Ta’awanu Association’s founder, Afif Abdel Rida Chouman, and two businessman brothers, Hassan Khechen and Ibrahim Khechen, accused of funnelling money from Iran to Hezbollah.

Two gold companies the brothers reportedly operate were added to the US sanctions list as well.

The administration of US President Donald Trump framed the added sanctions as part of its overarching effort to dismantle Hezbollah’s financial networks and cut off resources for Iran’s proxies.

“The Iranian regime’s attempts to infringe on Lebanon’s sovereignty through terror proxies like Hizballah will not be tolerated,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.

Since February 28, the US and its ally Israel have waged war against Iran, on the alleged premise that a military offensive was necessary to prevent Tehran from gaining nuclear weapons.

Iran, however, has long denied such ambitions, claiming its uranium enrichment programme is instead for civilian energy infrastructure.

Hezbollah, one of Iran’s regional allies, has been designated a “foreign terrorist organisation” in the US since 1997.

In Wednesday’s statement, the US Treasury accused civilian charitable organisations and humanitarian assistance efforts of channelling “outside donor funds toward Hezbollah’s terrorist activities”.

While Trump earlier this month claimed the conflict with Iran was “effectively over” from a military standpoint, US forces struck Iran’s Qeshm Island this week.

The US also continues to maintain a naval blockade, as well as an effort — dubbed Task Force Iron Gate — to prevent Iran from receiving supplies by land or the Caspian Sea.

To support that effort, the US aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt recently arrived in the Middle East.

Hours before Wednesday’s designations, the US military published a new advisory saying that it would treat ships receiving cargo at sea from vessels loaded in Iran as an attempt to evade its blockade. It warned it could take action against such vessels.

Last week, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told foreign ministers from the Group of Seven (G7) forum that the US would keep imposing “devastating” economic costs on Iran.

Hezbollah has denounced previous US sanctions, calling them an “attempt to intimidate the free Lebanese people”. It added that such economic penalties would have “absolutely no practical effect” on its “strategic choices”.

articles.title: Pat McAfee and crew roast ESPN's Heather Dinich for absurd College Football Playoff metrics
articles.summary: Pat McAfee's crew ripped ESPN's Heather Dinich over her "Strength of Conference" metric as College Football Playoff rankings spark SEC bias chatter.
articles.body: A lot has been made about the latest College Football Playoff rankings, though when is that ever not the case? I'm not here to discuss whether or not the powers that be are in cahoots with any one conference or if ESPN is exhibiting "SEC bias," but there seems to be a lot of chatter on social media, almost too much to ignore. Most of this stems from The Worldwide Leader's wrap-up coverage from Tuesday night's CFP rankings reveal, during which ESPN's Heather Dinich unveiled a new metric called "Strength of Conference." ESPN'S HEATHER DINICH DESTROYED BY CFB FANS OVER MYSTERY PLAYOFF RANKING METRIC, UCLA CHEERLEADERS & TARPS OFF Dinich took plenty of heat for this, most of which came from fans online, but one prominent voice that works for the very same network may have just fired off a shot inside the ESPN tent. Pat McAfee had Reece Davis on to make sense of what many are calling the most confusing CFP rankings in the history of the sport, and after Davis exited stage right, the boys took their own employer to task. "It is hard not to just be like, 'there's a lot of SEC representation in there,'" McAfee said. He also pointed out that there are plenty of SEC athletic directors who are on the CFP selection committee, and that Mark Dantonio might need to start "swinging a bit bigger fist." NEW COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF POLL PROVES THE SELECTION COMMITTEE IS JUST MAKING IT UP AS THEY GO That's when Ty Schmitt, one of McAfee's crew members, dropped the bomb, referring to Dinich as a "turncoat." McAfee let out a sarcastic "no," before a voice off camera accused her of "making up new metrics." "She couldn't explain it worth a damn," Schmitt said. Obviously, the ribbing is mostly tongue-in-cheek from McAfee and crew, and if Dinich were on set with them, they’d be dishing it out right to her face. I don't think there's anything nefarious going on here, but it is funny to see even people within the ESPN umbrella pushing the narrative that the CFP committee is compromised. I wonder if Pat will be receiving a call from some of the higher-ups telling him to tone it down? I digress. Again, I'm not here to make a stink of the CFP rankings. I'll leave that to guys like Ian Miller (also, my Florida Gators are part of the problem as a ranked four-loss team, so I must recuse myself). Suffice to say, we have a few weeks left until these rankings are actually final, so if I were you all, I'd save my breath until things are written in stone. articles.title: What is happening with the Scottish government's bonds?
articles.summary: MSPs have heard both the pros and cons of the government's plan to launch its first ever bond to the market?
articles.body:
The Scottish government is facing questions about its plan to issue its first ever bonds.

The move would allow ministers to borrow money from investors who in return receive regular interest payments.

The aim is to raise about £1.5bn by the end of the parliamentary term, with the funds to be used on long-term projects such as building hospitals or maintaining roads.

Named "kilts", a nod to UK government "gilts", the scheme has provoked much debate.

This week, MSPs on Holyrood's finance committee heard about the potential risks and rewards.

A bond is a financial tool used by a government to borrow money. They are sold with a promise for the buyer, or investor, to be paid back at the end of an agreed term.

The government will also make regular payments to the investor.

In the UK, a government bond is called a gilt. They are typically bought by financial institutions such as pension funds, insurance companies and commercial banks.

As a play on this term, the Scottish bonds have been nicknamed "kilts".

The Scottish government has said it expects the bonds to be issued within this financial year, subject to market conditions.

Former First Minister Humza Yousaf commissioned initial work in 2023 after advisers in the Scottish government's Investor Panel recommended making bonds available to the market as a means of raising Scotland's profile and attracting investment.

In November last year, the government announced that it had received an identical credit rating to the UK's score.

This was based on "prudent fiscal management" and the country's economic stability - though ministers were warned this could change if Scotland moved towards independence.

With market volatility due to conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, some have questioned whether now is a good time to launch bonds.

But at Holyrood, David McMillan, professor in finance and accounting at the University of Stirling, told MSPs: "You can't wait for a perfect time because there's going to be no perfect time."

The government wants to raise £1.5bn through bonds by 2031, although that would only be a fraction of its near £70bn budget.

About four-fifths of the Scottish government's budget is used on resource spending, which goes towards day-to-day costs such as funding the NHS, benefits payments and paying salaries.

A smaller portion is made up of capital spending, typically used on long-term physical assets such as buildings and bridges, or maintaining roads or paths.

The Scottish government is unable to borrow for resource spending other than to correct forecasting errors.

However, for capital spending, it can borrow as much as £450m a year at 2023-24 levels up to a total cap of £3bn - to be uprated with inflation.

Adjusted for inflation, the government could borrow about £491m in the current financial year, with a total limit of about £3.3bn.

Economists have noted that Scottish bonds would be a more costly way of borrowing than existing routes provided by the UK government through the National Loans Fund.

It has been estimated that interest rates on "kilts" would be 0.3 percentage points above gilts, plus an additional £2m per bond in administrative costs.

The Scottish government has not released costings, citing market sensitivities, but has insisted issuing bonds would represent value for money relative to the costs of borrowing through the UK scheme.

Ministers argue that issuing bonds would be a good opportunity to market the country to investors, and would be helpful if Scotland became independent.

Dr Ben Cormier, a senior lecturer at the University of Strathclyde's department of government and public policy, told Holyrood's finance committee that while the Scottish bonds could cost marginally more than the UK scheme, they would "bring flexibility to public finances and debt management".

McMillan agreed with the plans "in principle", but warned they would lose "credibility" with investors if limited to five years.

Cormier warned that independence was the one thing "that could materially change the nature of risk associated with Scottish bonds".

Conservative MSP Liam Kerr said bonds could be more expensive than borrowing through the National Loans Fund and voiced concerns about a lack of transparency in the programme.

McMillan agreed there should be "full information" available, saying: "You've got to have a clear, full and frank conversation with the public."

articles.body: A woman in her 70s from Newry has lost upwards of £250,000 after investing in what she believed was a cryptocurrency scheme advertised online, the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) has said. Police received the report on Thursday 21 May. According to Detective Inspector Moffett, she initially sent a relatively small amount, then sent larger sums after being convinced she needed to do so to recover her investment. She also unknowingly downloaded malware at the criminals’ instruction, which police believe allowed them to control her devices and transfer further sums from her account.How scammers stole over £250,000 through a cryptocurrency schemeAccording to Detective Inspector Moffett, the woman first sent a relatively small amount of money. She then "invested" larger amounts on several occasions after the criminals convinced her that she needed to send more to get her initial investment back. Moffett received the initial small payment and the later, larger sums sent to recover her original money.As per the PSNI Police statement, the woman unknowingly downloaded malware at the criminals' instruction. Detective Inspector Moffett said this allowed them to gain control of her electronic devices and, police believe, to transfer further sums from her account.PSNI urges families to protect relatives from cryptocurrency fraudSuperintendent Joanne Gibson, Chair of the Scamwise Partnership, said that taking a moment to stop and check any financial activity can make a real difference. According to the PSNI, she said the service will use every available resource to protect individuals and communities from the harm caused by fraud and exploitation. She also asked family members to take the time to talk with relatives about fraud, in an effort to safeguard them against criminals.Superintendent Gibson said that this type of crime can have a far-reaching impact and that people can work together to protect and prevent it from happening to those they care about. She added that fraudsters can be extremely convincing and use a variety of scenarios to make people believe they are genuine. The PSNI also quotes her as saying that anyone concerned about the intent of a person involved with someone they care about can report this to police on the non-emergency number 101. She said police "will listen and will act", and that any abuse of that trust will be treated with the utmost seriousness.Police urge people to verify callers before transferring moneyThe PSNI statement says that anyone who has received unsolicited calls, emails or letters should report this to Report Fraud. They can also call police on 101. The PSNI also says people should report any suspected fraudulent financial activity to their bank at the first opportunity, so that the bank can take action.The PSNI sets out its "Stop. Think Fraud" advice in two parts. "Stop" means pausing before transferring money or disclosing personal details to anyone you do not know, and not feeling rushed or pressured by timelines, because genuine callers will always give you time to consider your options. "Think Fraud" means checking and verifying who you are communicating with through a trusted source, verifying callers on another phone line where possible, and checking images with an image search. articles.title: A venture that turns discarded temple flowers into an alternative to leather now processes 50 tonnes a day across four Indian states; it has secured $6 million in debt financing from three Indian banks
articles.summary: For many devotees, flowers are an offering made with faith. But once a prayer is over, those same flowers often lose their purpose.
articles.body: For many devotees, flowers are an offering made with faith. But once a prayer is over, those same flowers often lose their purpose. In many places, they are discarded into rivers or left in heaps of waste, becoming part of an environmental problem that receives little attention.For entrepreneur Ankit Agarwal, this contrast became difficult to ignore. During a visit to the banks of the Ganga in Kanpur on Makar Sankranti in 2015, he noticed flowers used in religious offerings being thrown into the river. What others might have considered an ordinary sight stayed with him. He began wondering whether these flowers could be put to another use instead of becoming waste.That question eventually led to the creation of Phool, a venture that collects discarded temple flowers and turns them into products such as incense and a leather alternative. Today, the business processes around 50 tonnes of floral waste every day across four Indian states. It has also secured $6 million in debt financing from the Export-Import Bank of India, the Small Industries Development Bank of India and ICICI Bank, announced at The Earthshot Prize's Impact Assembly in Mumbai. But behind the numbers is a story about noticing a problem that had become so familiar that few stopped to question it.An everyday sight that became a difficult questionAgarwal's idea did not begin with a business plan or a ready-made solution. It began with a simple observation: flowers offered with devotion were ending up in a polluted river. He started exploring ways to collect and reuse them. He later joined hands with his childhood friend Prateek Kumar, an environmental engineer, to work on the idea. Their venture, Kanpur Flowercycling Private Limited, was incorporated in 2017.The early work involved more than figuring out how to make something from flowers. The founders also had to build a system to collect the offerings from temples, sort the material and transport it for processing. This meant convincing religious institutions to participate and developing a regular supply chain for something that was usually treated as waste. Their first products included incense sticks and cones made from discarded flowers. The idea offered a way to give the material another purpose while creating work around its collection and processing.When flower waste became something unexpectedAs the team continued experimenting with floral waste, it came across another possibility. A mat-like layer formed over unused flower fibres at the factory. Instead of treating it as an unwanted by-product, the founders explored whether it could be developed into a leather-like material.This eventually became Fleather, a material made from discarded flowers and developed as an alternative to conventional animal leather. It opened up possibilities beyond incense, particularly in products that use leather or similar materials. The innovation brought the venture international attention. In 2022, its Fleather initiative became a finalist for the Earthshot Prize in the Build a Waste-Free World category.There is also a human side to the collection process. The venture has employed women from marginalised communities in collecting and processing flowers, offering livelihood opportunities through work that begins with material otherwise thrown away. For these workers, the discarded offerings are not simply an environmental concern. They can become a source of income, connecting the idea of waste recovery with everyday livelihoods.From a local experiment to a wider operationThe scale of the venture has changed considerably since those early experiments in Kanpur. According to The Earthshot Prize, its daily floral-waste processing capacity has grown from 36 tonnes across two states in 2022 to 50 tonnes across four states. The latest development is the $6 million debt financing announced at the Mumbai Impact Assembly. The funding comes from three Indian banks: Exim Bank, SIDBI and ICICI Bank. Since this is debt financing rather than an equity investment or grant, it is money the business is expected to repay under agreed terms.The announcement was part of a wider set of environmental partnerships unveiled at the assembly. Global companies including Amazon, NVIDIA, Uber and IKEA were among those joining efforts with Earthshot Prize winners and finalists. The initiatives covered areas such as cleaner air, climate resilience, ocean protection and sustainable transport. For Agarwal's venture, the funding marks an important stage in its growth. But expanding a model built around waste collection also involves practical challenges: securing a consistent supply of flowers, managing transportation, maintaining product quality and finding buyers for the finished materials.The bigger story behind the flowersDiscarded temple flowers are only one part of India's wider waste challenge. Turning them into useful products does not solve every problem associated with river pollution or agricultural and urban waste. Nor does a growing processing capacity automatically mean that all floral waste is being collected. Still, Agarwal's journey raises a useful question about the things people routinely throw away. What happens when someone looks at waste not as the end of a material's usefulness, but as the beginning of another possibility?For the workers involved in collecting and processing the flowers, it can mean a livelihood. For the founders, it has meant years of experimentation and building a collection network. And for the communities around the rivers, it offers one possible way to reduce the burden of discarded offerings. The idea began with a sight on the banks of the Ganga that many people may have walked past. Its next chapter will depend on whether this model can grow while keeping its environmental and social purpose at the centre.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
